question: Aryana controls [Ascended Lawmage] and [Cemetery Gate]. Nicholas controls [Onakke Ogre] enchanted by their [Paralyze]. Aryana casts [Sudden Disappearance] targeting Nicholas. When the trigger resolves at the beginning of the next end step, what can Paralyze enchant?
answer:
Paralyze can be attached to either Onakke Ogre or Aryana's Ascended Lawmage — Nicholas chooses as Paralyze enters the battlefield. It cannot be attached to Cemetery Gate.

Why:

- Sudden Disappearance exiled every nonland permanent Nicholas controlled, which includes both Onakke Ogre and Paralyze. At the beginning of the next end step they all return to the battlefield together under their owner's control, so Paralyze returns under Nicholas's control.
- Paralyze is entering the battlefield by an effect other than resolving as an Aura spell, and Sudden Disappearance doesn't specify what Paralyze will enchant. Under rule 303.4f, Paralyze's controller (Nicholas) chooses what it enchants as it enters, and that choice must be legal according to Paralyze's "Enchant creature" ability and any other applicable effects. Since the returning cards all enter at the same time, Onakke Ogre is on the battlefield to be chosen; it is a perfectly legal choice.
- Ascended Lawmage is a legal choice too. Its hexproof only means it "can't be the target of spells or abilities your opponents control" (702.11b). Attaching Paralyze as it enters the battlefield doesn't target anything, so hexproof doesn't prevent it. Note Nicholas would then control an Aura on Aryana's creature — that's fine.
- Cemetery Gate is not a legal choice. It has protection from black, and Paralyze is a black Aura (mana cost {B}), so Cemetery Gate can't be enchanted by it (702.16c). If Paralyze somehow became attached to Cemetery Gate anyway, it would be put into Nicholas's graveyard as a state-based action (704.5m, 303.4c).
- If for some reason there were no legal creature at all, Paralyze would simply remain in exile rather than entering the battlefield (303.4g).

Once attached, Paralyze's enters ability triggers and taps whatever creature it's now enchanting.

One assumption on timing: I'm assuming Sudden Disappearance's delayed triggered ability resolves normally and returns everything simultaneously. If that delayed trigger were countered or removed from the stack, the cards would stay in exile indefinitely and Paralyze would never enter, so the question wouldn't arise. If somehow Onakke Ogre didn't come back with Paralyze, Ascended Lawmage would be the only legal choice among the creatures listed.

Multiplayer note: with only Aryana and Nicholas, the choices are as above. At a larger table the same rules apply to every creature on the battlefield, with one extra restriction — an Aura can't enchant an object outside its controller's range of influence (801.8), which matters only in formats that use a limited range of influence.

question: Ayla controls [Living Plane] and plays [Minas Tirith]. Does it enter tapped or untapped?
answer:
Minas Tirith enters tapped — unless Ayla already controls some other legendary creature on the battlefield at that moment. Minas Tirith cannot satisfy its own condition, even though Living Plane will make it a legendary 1/1 creature land.

Why:

- "Minas Tirith enters tapped unless you control a legendary creature" is a static ability that replaces how the permanent enters the battlefield; it applies as part of the event that puts Minas Tirith onto the battlefield, not as a triggered ability afterward [603.6d]. Absent such an effect, permanents enter untapped [110.5b].
- The condition is checked as Minas Tirith is entering, and the required legendary creature must already be on the battlefield at that time. A permanent entering the battlefield at the same time doesn't count [Minas Tirith ruling #1]. Minas Tirith is, of course, entering simultaneously with itself, so it can't be the legendary creature that turns off its own "enters tapped" clause.
- Living Plane's effect ("All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands") does apply to Minas Tirith the instant it's on the battlefield, and never before then [603.6b]. Rule 614.12 does say to check the entering permanent's characteristics as they would exist on the battlefield, taking pre-existing continuous effects into account — so Minas Tirith is indeed a legendary land creature once it's there — but that only settles what Minas Tirith itself looks like; it doesn't put Minas Tirith onto the battlefield early so it can be counted as "a legendary creature you control" for its own check [614.12]. The card-specific ruling governs the timing here.
- Important corollary: because Living Plane turns every land into a creature, any other legendary land Ayla already controls is a legendary creature. So if Ayla controls, say, another legendary land (or any ordinary legendary creature) before playing Minas Tirith, Minas Tirith enters untapped.
- Timing note: I'm assuming Living Plane is already on the battlefield and resolved before Minas Tirith is played, as stated. If instead Living Plane were entering simultaneously with Minas Tirith, nothing would be a creature at the check either, and Minas Tirith would still enter tapped unless another legendary creature was already present.

Player count doesn't change any of this: "you control a legendary creature" only looks at Ayla's own permanents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: Nixon has a [Southern Elephant] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Addison casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nixon. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nixon know which manifested card is which?
answer:
**The three +1/+1 counters stay on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave the whole way, so it hits the battlefield as a face-down 5/5 — and that instantly gives it away. Nixon (and everyone else) will know which manifested permanent is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is Southern Elephant.**

Why the counters survive:

- Normally counters simply cease to exist when an object changes zones [122.2]. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text overrides that general rule: "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Card text beats the general rule here.
- Ghastly Conscription moves the card graveyard → exile → battlefield. Neither destination is a hand or library, and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave still has its abilities in the graveyard and in exile (a card exiled face down is merely hidden from view [406.3]; that doesn't strip its abilities). The retention ability only needs to be active in the zone the card is leaving [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2], so it applies on both moves, and it retains all kinds of counters, not just +1/+1 ones [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #6].

Why that reveals it:

- A manifested card is put onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature with no name, no text, no subtypes, and no mana cost [701.40a], [708.2], [708.2a], [Ghastly Conscription ruling #9]. The three +1/+1 counters that rode along add +3/+3 [122.1a], so the face-down Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is a 5/5 with three visible counters, while the face-down Southern Elephant is a plain 2/2. Counters sit on top of the permanent in public view, so the shuffle of the face-down pile — whose whole purpose is to disguise which manifested card is which [Ghastly Conscription ruling #4] — fails for Skullbriar, the Walking Grave.

Other practical points:

- Addison cast Ghastly Conscription, so Addison controls both manifested permanents and may look at them [Ghastly Conscription ruling #14]; Nixon may not look at them, but doesn't need to — the counters identify Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. Addison can turn the creature cards face up for their mana costs as a special action ({B}{G} for Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, {3}{G} for Southern Elephant) [Ghastly Conscription ruling #3].
- Note the counters weren't "put" on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave — they just persisted — so counter-doubling/prevention effects don't interact with them [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1].
- Caution for later: while it's face down it has no abilities [708.2a], so it no longer has the retention text. If that face-down permanent leaves the battlefield while still face down, the counters would cease to exist [122.2].

Nothing above depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Nixon's graveyard is targeted and Addison controls the resulting manifests.

question: Asa controls [Library of Leng] and is discarding a card due to [Azra Oddsmaker]'s ability. Can they put the discarded card on top of their library? If so, what happens?
answer:
No — Asa must put the discarded card into their graveyard. Library of Leng does not apply to the discard from Azra Oddsmaker's ability, because that discard is a cost, not an effect.

Why: Azra Oddsmaker's triggered ability reads "At the beginning of combat on your turn, you may discard a card. If you do, choose a creature...." That is exactly the template covered by rule 118.12 — "[A player] may [do something]. If [that player] [does]..." — which states that the "[do something]" action is a cost, paid as the ability resolves. Library of Leng's replacement applies only "If an effect causes you to discard a card," and effects are what spells and abilities create as they resolve (rule 609.1). The card's own ruling settles it directly: you can't use Library of Leng to put a discarded card on top of your library when you discard as a cost, because costs aren't effects [Library of Leng ruling #5].

So the sequence is: Azra Oddsmaker's ability resolves, Asa chooses to pay the discard cost, the card goes from hand to graveyard (it still counts as a discard and will set off any "whenever a player discards" triggers, per [Library of Leng ruling #3]), and because Asa did pay, they then choose a creature; that creature gets "Whenever that creature deals combat damage to a player this turn, you draw two cards."

Related point on the "if you do" clause: rule 118.12 checks whether the player started to pay the cost, and rule 118.11 says the cost still counts as paid even if effects modify the actions performed. So even in cases where a replacement effect changes what actually happens to the discarded card, the "If you do" clause would still be satisfied — the choosing of a creature is never in danger here.

Contrast: if some other spell or ability instructed Asa to discard as part of its resolution (an effect, e.g. "discard a card, then draw a card"), Library of Leng would let Asa put that card on top of their library instead of into the graveyard [Library of Leng ruling #4].

Player count doesn't matter: Azra Oddsmaker's trigger and Library of Leng only involve Asa, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Albert, Brielle, and Campbell are playing a multiplayer game. Brielle controls [Stalking Leonin]. Albert casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Brielle's next turn. After Brielle begins their turn, can Albert see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
answer:
Yes. Once Brielle's controlled turn begins, Albert can see which opponent Brielle secretly chose for Stalking Leonin.

Why: Rule 723.4 says that if information about an object in the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it's visible to both that player and the controller of that player. The secret choice made when Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield is information about an object in the game (Stalking Leonin itself) that Brielle can see — for example, the piece of paper with the chosen player's name kept with Stalking Leonin, one of the suggested methods in the Stalking Leonin rulings. So during the turn Albert controls Brielle, that hidden information is open to Albert as well. The Worst Fears rulings say the same thing for cards: while controlling another player you can see all cards in the game that player can see, including their hand and face-down permanents they control (rule 723.4). The one carve-out is information about cards *outside* the game (sideboard, "choose a card from outside the game") — that stays visible only to Brielle.

Practical consequences during that turn:
- Albert makes Brielle's choices and decisions, including whether to activate Stalking Leonin's last ability, and he must use only Brielle's resources to pay Brielle's costs (rules 723.5, 723.5a). Note that the ability's cost is "Reveal the player you chose," and it can only exile a creature attacking Brielle that's controlled by the player Brielle chose — Albert can't change that choice, since it was locked in when Stalking Leonin entered (Stalking Leonin ruling on not having chosen an opponent).
- Albert does not control Stalking Leonin itself; all permanents remain under their normal controllers, and Brielle is still the active player on their own turn (rule 723.3).
- Albert also keeps making his own choices and decisions as a player (rule 723.8).

Multiplayer note: this is already a three-player game, and nothing changes here versus a two-player game except that Brielle's "chosen opponent" for Stalking Leonin could be Albert or Campbell — and Albert now knows which. Also, since Brielle is the controlled active player, APNAP order (rule 101.4b) still runs from Brielle, with Albert making Brielle's choices at Brielle's spot in turn order and his own at his own spot.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Stalking Leonin's opponent was chosen before Albert's Worst Fears turn began; the visibility is the same regardless, but Albert only gets to see it while the control effect is active — it lasts the entire turn and ends at the beginning of the following turn (rule 723.1).

question: Abdullah controls [Primal Vigor] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Primal Vigor to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield with exactly one +1/+1 counter, not two.

Why: both abilities are replacement effects that modify how Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield. Rescuer Sphinx's "As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it" is a replacement effect ([614.1c]), and Primal Vigor's "If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature, twice that many +1/+1 counters are put on that creature instead" is also a replacement effect ([614.1a]) that does apply to counters a permanent enters the battlefield with ([122.6a], [Primal Vigor ruling #3]).

The order is forced here. Primal Vigor has nothing to replace until there is an event of putting +1/+1 counters on Rescuer Sphinx, and that event only exists once Rescuer Sphinx's own replacement effect has been applied and Abdullah has actually chosen to return a permanent. So Rescuer Sphinx's effect is applied first; Abdullah returns Primal Vigor to hand as part of applying it. Then the process repeats, taking into account only the replacement effects that are now applicable ([616.1], [616.1f]) — and Primal Vigor is no longer on the battlefield, so its doubling effect isn't there to apply. The single counter is not doubled.

Timing note: Rescuer Sphinx's ruling confirms the choice and the return happen while Rescuer Sphinx is entering, and that no player may act between choosing the permanent to return and Rescuer Sphinx being on the battlefield with its +1/+1 counter ([Rescuer Sphinx ruling #3]). Under either reading of the exact instant — Primal Vigor leaving as the replacement is applied, or the counter being placed at the moment Rescuer Sphinx arrives — Primal Vigor is already in Abdullah's hand and doubles nothing. The only way to get two counters is to return some other nonland permanent and leave Primal Vigor on the battlefield; the check for which effects apply is made against how Rescuer Sphinx would exist on the battlefield taking already-applied modifications into account ([614.12]).

Player count doesn't change this. Only Abdullah is making choices, so the APNAP ordering in [616.1] never comes up, and Primal Vigor works regardless of who controls the creature getting counters ([Primal Vigor ruling #2]) — the answer is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

question: Anderson controls [Quirion Explorer]. Nico controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Anderson taps Quirion Explorer, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Anderson may add one mana of any one color he chooses — {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}. He cannot add {C} with Quirion Explorer, because {C} is colorless mana, not a color, and Quirion Explorer only offers "one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce."

Why: Rule [106.7] defines what a permanent "could produce" as any type of mana that *an ability of that permanent* would produce if that ability were to resolve at that time, ignoring whether its costs could be paid. It is not limited to activated mana abilities. Crumbling Vestige has two mana-producing abilities: the triggered ability "When this land enters, add one mana of any color," and "{T}: Add {C}." The {T} ability would only make colorless mana, which is not a color and so gives Quirion Explorer nothing. The enters-the-battlefield ability, hypothetically resolving now, would produce one mana of any color, so all five colors are types Crumbling Vestige could produce, and Anderson picks one of those five when Quirion Explorer's ability resolves.

The alternate reading, for completeness: if you count only Crumbling Vestige's {T}: Add {C} ability, then no color would be defined and Quirion Explorer would produce no mana at all under [106.5] and the last sentence of [106.7] — Quirion Explorer's own ruling confirms the ability can still be activated in that case, it just produces nothing. The rules text of [106.7] does not restrict the check to activated abilities, so the five-color answer is the one supported by the rule as written. Also note [605.2]: Quirion Explorer's ability is a mana ability regardless of whether the game state lets it make mana, so it never uses the stack and can't be responded to.

Timing doesn't matter here: whether Crumbling Vestige entered turns ago or its enter trigger is still waiting to resolve, [106.7] asks a hypothetical question about what its abilities would produce, so the answer is the same.

Multiplayer: Quirion Explorer reads "a land an opponent controls," so at a table with more than two players Anderson checks the lands of *every* opponent, not just Nico — any color any of those lands could produce is available. With just Anderson and Nico, Crumbling Vestige is the only source being checked.

question: Andi controls [Karn Liberated], which has exiled an [Anvil of Bogardan]. They activate Karn Liberated's -14 ability, and restarts the game. How many cards will they draw during their first turn?
answer:
Two-player game: Andi draws zero cards during their first turn. Multiplayer game (three or more players): Andi draws two cards (their normal draw plus Anvil of Bogardan's extra card), then discards one.

Why:

1. Karn Liberated's −14 restarts the game, and the player who controlled the ability that restarted the game is the starting player in the new game [727.1a]. So Andi takes the first turn.

2. Anvil of Bogardan is a non-Aura permanent card exiled with Karn Liberated, so it stays in exile through the restart and is then put onto the battlefield under Andi's control. That happens as Karn Liberated's ability finishes resolving, just before the first turn's untap step [727.4], so Anvil of Bogardan is already on the battlefield when Andi's draw step would occur [Karn Liberated ruling #5], [Karn Liberated ruling #3].

3. In a two-player game, the player who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn [103.8a]. To skip a step is to proceed past it as though it didn't exist [500.11], and anything scheduled for a skipped step simply won't happen [614.10a]. Since the draw step never occurs, Anvil of Bogardan's "At the beginning of each player's draw step" ability never triggers at all — so there's no extra draw and no discard either. (Anvil of Bogardan's ruling that the discard still happens when the draw is skipped applies when a replacement effect skips just the card draw, not when the entire draw step is skipped.) Andi draws no cards during that turn; the seven cards in their opening hand come from the pregame procedure, not from a draw during the turn [Karn Liberated ruling #10].

4. With more than two players, rule 103.8a's skip applies only "in a two-player game," so the starting player does not skip their draw step. Andi would draw their one card for the turn, then Anvil of Bogardan's trigger resolves for an additional draw and a discard — two cards drawn, one discarded. (Note that Anvil of Bogardan's trigger goes on the stack after the turn-based draw has already happened [Anvil of Bogardan ruling #4].)

Also worth noting: any player who had already left the game before the restart isn't part of the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #12].

question: At the beginning of the game, Alianna announced [Zirda, the Dawnwaker] as their companion. During the game, Alianna cast [Glistening Goremonger] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alianna restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: the game ends immediately and a new game starts with Alianna as the starting player. The Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger card that Alianna brought in from outside the game with Wish is now "involved in the game," so it becomes part of Alianna's library in the new game — it does not go back to the sideboard. Zirda, the Dawnwaker, which never left the outside-the-game zone, is still outside the game, and Alianna may reveal it as their companion again during the new game's pregame procedure — but only if the new starting deck (which now contains Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger) still satisfies Zirda, the Dawnwaker's condition.

Details:

1. Restarting. Karn Liberated's −14 ends the current game with no winner, loser, or drawer, and all players still in the game immediately begin a new one following the normal pregame procedure of rule 103 [727.1, 104.6, Karn Liberated ruling #13]. Nothing that happened in the old game carries over [Karn Liberated ruling #2], and Alianna (the controller of the restarting ability) is the starting player in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #10].

2. The Wish card. Every Magic card involved in the ended game is involved in the new game, even if it wasn't originally part of it; the rules give exactly this case as the example (a creature card fetched from outside the game with Living Wish ends up in that player's library in the new game) [727.2]. So Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger — the double-faced card whose front face Alianna cast off Wish — shuffles into Alianna's library, front face up, with no memory of having been transformed. Players also can't move cards between deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #6]. The one exception: if that card had instead been exiled by Karn Liberated's +4 or −3 as a non-Aura permanent card, it would stay in exile and be put onto the battlefield under Alianna's control after the pregame procedure [727.5, Karn Liberated ruling #5].

3. Zirda, the Dawnwaker. "Companion" is a keyword that functions outside the game: before the game begins you may reveal one card you own from outside the game whose companion condition your starting deck fulfills, and once per game you may pay {3} as a special action to put it into your hand [702.139a, 103.2b, 116.2g]. question: Amos controls [March of the Machines] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and casts [Lust for War] targeting their [Gilded Sentinel]. What will happen when Lust for War resolves?
answer:
Lust for War will resolve, briefly enter the battlefield attached to Gilded Sentinel, and then immediately be put into Amos's graveyard as a state-based action — it never gets to do anything.

Step by step:

1. **On the stack, Lust for War is safe.** Mycosynth Lattice only affects permanents; spells on the stack aren't permanents, so Lust for War is still just an Aura spell while it's being cast and is a legal spell targeting Gilded Sentinel, which is a legal creature to enchant [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2].

2. **It enters attached.** When Lust for War resolves it enters the battlefield attached to Gilded Sentinel, since Gilded Sentinel is a legal object for its "Enchant creature" ability [303.4i], [701.3a].

3. **Mycosynth Lattice makes Lust for War an artifact.** "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types," so Lust for War is now an artifact Enchantment — Aura (it keeps its prior types) [205.1b], [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #4]. It's also colorless from Mycosynth Lattice's second ability.

4. **March of the Machines animates it.** Lust for War is now a noncreature artifact, so March of the Machines makes it an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value. Lust for War's mana cost is {2}{R}, mana value 3, so it's a 3/3 — it keeps its enchantment and Aura types as well [March of the Machines ruling #2], [613.6].

5. **State-based actions kill it.** An Aura that's also a creature can't enchant anything: it becomes unattached, and then is put into its owner's graveyard as a second state-based action [303.4d], [704.5p], [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #4]. This happens the next time state-based actions are checked, before any player gets priority, so Lust for War's "attacks each combat if able" and its damage trigger never matter. Note it isn't dying to a 0-toughness check — a 3/3 is fine — it's dying specifically because a creature can't be an Aura attached to something.

Gilded Sentinel is unaffected: it was already an artifact creature, and March of the Machines only animates *noncreature* artifacts, so it stays a 3/3 Golem (now also colorless from Mycosynth Lattice). Amos has simply spent {2}{R} for nothing.

This result is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer — nothing here depends on opponents or turn order.

question: Allyson controls [Ice Cauldron]. Nico controls [Suppression Field]. Allyson activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Allyson's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?
answer:
Allyson adds {C}{C}{C} — three colorless mana — and that mana can be spent only to cast the card last exiled with Ice Cauldron.

Why: Suppression Field says "Activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they're mana abilities." Ice Cauldron's first ability ({X}, {T}: exile a nonland card, put a charge counter, note the mana spent) produces no mana, so it is not a mana ability and Suppression Field's increase applies. With X=1, the total cost of that activation was {1} + {2} from Suppression Field = {3} generic, which Allyson paid with {C}{C}{C} (colorless mana is a legal way to pay generic costs). Cost increases are applied when the total cost is determined and then locked in [601.2f], and activating an ability uses those same cost rules with the activation cost standing in for a mana cost [602.1a] [602.2b].

Ice Cauldron notes "the type and amount of mana spent to pay this activation cost" — that means what was actually spent, not the value of X. The ruling that Ice Cauldron "counts only mana spent on it. It doesn't see the value of X" [Ice Cauldron ruling #9] cuts both ways: just as cost reductions don't shrink the note, the extra {2} forced by Suppression Field is part of what was paid, so the noted amount is {C}{C}{C}, not a single mana.

On the second activation, Ice Cauldron's second ability ({T}, Remove a charge counter: Add this artifact's last noted type and amount of mana) is a mana ability [Ice Cauldron ruling #1], so Suppression Field explicitly does not increase its cost [Suppression Field ruling #1]. It adds the last noted mana — {C}{C}{C} — and because it's a mana ability it doesn't use the stack and resolves immediately, so it can't be responded to [605.3b] [405.6c]. That mana carries the restriction "Spend this mana only to cast the last card exiled with this artifact" [Ice Cauldron ruling #12]; Allyson may still add other mana from other sources to finish paying for that spell.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming the mana was noted at the time of the first activation with Suppression Field already on the battlefield. If Nico's Suppression Field had entered only after Allyson had already paid for the first ability, the noted amount would just be the {1} generic actually paid (e.g. {C}), and the second ability would add one mana of whatever type was spent.

Player count doesn't matter here: Suppression Field affects activated abilities regardless of who controls them, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Aubrey controls [Mycosynth Lattice]. Natalia controls [Watchwolf] enchanted with [Favorable Destiny]. Aubrey casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and takes control of Favorable Destiny. What will happen after Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves?
answer:
Favorable Destiny is put into Natalia's graveyard almost immediately. When Opportunistic Dragon's triggered ability resolves, Aubrey gains control of Favorable Destiny, Favorable Destiny loses all abilities, and it can't attack or block. Losing all abilities means Favorable Destiny loses its "Enchant creature" ability — and what an Aura may legally be attached to is defined solely by its enchant ability [303.4c, 702.5a]. With no enchant ability, Favorable Destiny is attached to an illegal object, so the next time state-based actions are checked (before any player receives priority) Favorable Destiny is put into its owner's graveyard [704.5m]. Its owner is Natalia, so it goes to Natalia's graveyard even though Aubrey controls it at that moment [110.2b].

Why Favorable Destiny was a legal target at all: Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types, so the enchantment Favorable Destiny is an artifact on the battlefield and qualifies as "target Human or artifact an opponent controls" [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2]. This mirrors the published Mycosynth Lattice ruling about Auras that stop being able to enchant anything: they become unattached and are put into their owner's graveyard as a state-based action [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #4].

Other consequences:
- Gaining control of Favorable Destiny does not move it and does not give Aubrey control of Watchwolf; an Aura's controller is separate from the enchanted permanent's controller [303.4e].
- While Favorable Destiny exists with no abilities, it grants nothing: Watchwolf loses the +1/+2 (which wasn't applying anyway, since Mycosynth Lattice makes Watchwolf colorless rather than white) and loses the conditional shroud. Watchwolf stays under Natalia's control and is unaffected once Favorable Destiny hits the graveyard.
- Note the shroud clause never protected Favorable Destiny itself — it only would have applied to Watchwolf.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Opportunistic Dragon is still on the battlefield when its trigger resolves. If Opportunistic Dragon leaves the battlefield before the ability resolves, Aubrey never gains control of Favorable Destiny, it doesn't lose any abilities, and it simply stays attached to Watchwolf [Opportunistic Dragon ruling #4].

Multiplayer: nothing changes. Opportunistic Dragon's trigger just requires the targeted artifact to be controlled by any one opponent of Aubrey, so with more than two players the same sequence occurs, and Favorable Destiny still goes to its own owner's graveyard [110.2b].

question: Amelia attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Shivan Meteor]?
answer:
No. As Wildfire Eternal's trigger resolves, Amelia can't suspend Shivan Meteor.

Why:

1. Exiling a card with suspend is a *special action*, not casting. "Suspend N—[cost]" means "If you could begin to cast this card by putting it onto the stack from your hand, you may pay [cost] and exile it with N time counters on it. This action doesn't use the stack" [702.62a], and taking that action is one of the twelve special actions, which a player may take "any time they have priority" [116.2f]. Shivan Meteor's own ruling confirms exiling a card with suspend isn't casting it and doesn't use the stack [Shivan Meteor ruling #3].

2. No player has priority while a spell or ability is resolving. During resolution, the only spell-casting allowed is what the resolving object specifically instructs or allows, and even then no player receives priority [608.2g]. Wildfire Eternal's trigger says "you may cast an instant or sorcery spell from your hand without paying its mana cost" — it grants permission to *cast*, not permission to take special actions. Since Amelia has no priority mid-resolution, the suspend special action simply isn't available then [116.2f], [608.2g].

What Amelia can do instead: Shivan Meteor is a sorcery in hand, so it's a legal choice for Wildfire Eternal's trigger — Amelia may cast Shivan Meteor from hand for free right then (during the declare blockers step), choosing its target at that time [Wildfire Eternal ruling #1]. Note that casting it "without paying its mana cost" means no alternative cost can be paid [Wildfire Eternal ruling #7], and paying the suspend cost {1}{R}{R} isn't an option here regardless, because suspending isn't casting at all.

If Amelia declines the trigger, Shivan Meteor stays in hand and they can suspend it later at a time they have priority and could begin to cast it — for a sorcery that means during one of their own main phases with the stack empty [702.62a], [Shivan Meteor ruling #12]. Suspending it then costs {1}{R}{R} and exiles it with two time counters.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading the question as asking about the moment Wildfire Eternal's "attacks and isn't blocked" trigger is actually resolving [Wildfire Eternal ruling #5]. If instead you meant while the trigger is on the stack (i.e., anyone still holding priority in the declare blockers step), the answer is still no for Shivan Meteor specifically — Amelia would have priority, but suspend requires that they could begin to cast the card, and a sorcery can't be cast during combat with a trigger on the stack [702.62a], [702.62c], [Shivan Meteor ruling #12].

Player count doesn't change any of this: the same priority and special-action rules apply in two-player and multiplayer games alike.

question: Autumn casts [Time Stretch]. Can they choose to skip both extra turns with [Time Vault]?
answer:
No — with a single Time Vault, Autumn can skip only one of the two extra turns (unless they can re-tap Time Vault, and there's no window to do so in between).

Why:

1. Time Stretch reads "Target player takes two extra turns after this one," so two extra turns are added directly after the current turn; extra turns are added one at a time, and the most recently created turn is taken first [500.7], [Time Stretch ruling #1].

2. Time Vault's last ability reads "If you would begin your turn while this artifact is tapped, you may skip that turn instead. If you do, untap this artifact." To skip a turn is to proceed past it as though it didn't exist [500.11]; "skip" effects are replacement effects, and the choice is made as the turn would begin, only if Time Vault is tapped at that moment [614.10], [614.10a], [614.1b], [Time Vault ruling #1].

3. Assume Time Vault is tapped when the first extra turn would begin. Autumn may choose to skip that first extra turn — and as part of that same replacement, Time Vault untaps ("If you do, untap this artifact"), and it untaps before anything else happens [Time Vault ruling #1].

4. The second extra turn from Time Stretch then would begin immediately. Time Vault is now untapped, so the condition "while this artifact is tapped" isn't met and the skip option simply isn't available. Nothing happens during a skipped turn — it never occurs, so Autumn never gets priority in it to activate anything [614.10a]. Time Vault also "doesn't untap during your untap step," but that's irrelevant here; the problem is that it's already untapped.

5. Could Autumn tap it again first? Only by activating Time Vault's "{T}: Take an extra turn after this one" during a turn in which they have priority — but that activation creates yet another extra turn, which, being created most recently, is taken before Time Stretch's turns [500.7], [Time Stretch ruling #1]. So each tap of Time Vault buys one skip and simultaneously adds one more extra turn; the errata'd wording specifically prevents skipping multiple turns off repeated activations [Time Vault ruling #2].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Time Stretch resolves during Autumn's turn (it's a sorcery) and that Time Vault is tapped at the moment the first extra turn would begin. If Time Vault is untapped at that moment, Autumn can't skip the first extra turn at all; if Autumn instead activates Time Vault after Time Stretch resolves, the Time Vault extra turn is the one taken first (and is the one that can be skipped), with Time Stretch's two turns following unskippable.

Player count: This works the same at two players and at a multiplayer table, since both extra turns belong to Autumn. In multiplayer, if several players are given extra turns, they're added one at a time in APNAP order [500.7]. Under the shared team turns option, Autumn's team takes the extra turns and Autumn's team does the skipping [805.8]. In Grand Melee, extra turns depend on turn markers — an extra turn can be delayed until Autumn next holds a marker [807.4i], [807.4j].
